scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tribal Fusion emerged in the late 1990s in California as a departure from American Tribal Style (ATS).
Jill Parker’s company, Ultra Gypsy, is credited with initiating this shift by experimenting with theatrical themes and modern music.
The form was further popularized by Rachel Brice, who bridged the gap between ATS and a more individualized, fusion-based aesthetic.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tribal Fusion is performed at festivals, haflas, and theatrical venues.
It is a secular, artistic pursuit focused on individual expression and the synthesis of global dance traditions rather than the recreation of specific cultural rituals.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Belly Dance: Cues and Tattoos Festival 2015 - Bindu Bolar Tribalina. (https://archive.org/details/cues-and-tattoos-festival-2015-bindu-bolar-tribalina)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by sharp, muscular isolations and a fusion of belly dance with popping, hip-hop, and classical dance forms.
Unlike ATS, which relies on group improvisation and coded signals, Tribal Fusion is typically choreographed.
Dancers may perform as soloists or in groups, with movements ranging from fluid, traditional belly dance undulations to staccato, modern-dance-inspired isolations.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The genre is closely linked to electronic and world music.
Early contributors included DJs like Cheb i Sabbah and Bassnectar, while producers like Jeremiah Soto (Solace) and Karim Nagi helped define the 'Electronica Oriental' sound.
Listen for the Electronic synthesizers, Tabla, Global folk instruments.
A fusion of traditional Middle Eastern-derived rhythms with modern electronic breakbeats, bass-heavy production, and global instrumentation.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes vary from traditional tribal elements—such as antique silver jewelry, cholis, and cowrie shells—to minimalist, contemporary designs.
Influences from flamenco, burlesque, and other performance arts often dictate the choice of fabrics, feathers, and accessories.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Jill Parker, Rachel Brice, Mardi Love, Heather Stants, Zoe Jakes, and Ariellah Aflalo.
The lineage traces back to Jamila Salimpour and Masha Archer.
Subgenres include Dark Fusion, Vaudeville bellydance, Steampunk, Art Nouveau, and Urban Tribal, each incorporating different aesthetic and musical influences.

The lineage flows from Jamila Salimpour (Bal Anat) to Masha Archer (San Francisco Classic Dance Troupe), to Carolena Nericcio (FatChance BellyDance), to Jill Parker (Ultra Gypsy), and subsequently to modern pioneers like Rachel Brice and The Indigo.
